candidateRows: Early Pauline material supplies widely accepted testimony and traditions supporting a cumulative historical case for Jesus's resurrection.
This establishes the affirmative's overarching historical method and identifies crucifixion, resurrection claims, appearances, and Christianity's expansion as the cumulative explanatory case.
At the beginning of the substantive discussion, Bass defines scholarly common ground and outlines the principal facts from which his resurrection argument will proceed.
The reported appearances form cumulative testimony whose multiplicity and early accessibility make the resurrection claim historically compelling.
The motion expressly turns on early appearances, and this move gives the affirmative's main reason for treating them as mutually reinforcing historical testimony.
After agreement on crucifixion and the existence of resurrection claims, the discussion turns to what the reported appearances contribute to the affirmative explanation.
Only Paul's experience is directly self-attested, while the other appearance reports depend on indirect sources that require ordinary reliability analysis.
This directly contests the affirmative's cumulative eyewitness foundation by challenging source access and demanding equal treatment of comparable religious testimony.
Bass's claim that four individual appearance witnesses constitute widely accepted bedrock eyewitness evidence.
Following Bass's enumeration of individual witnesses, Ehrman grants some experiences as probable but argues that historians lack direct testimony from most named figures.
Mormon witness testimony supplies a religious comparison that tests whether the resurrection case applies eyewitness standards impartially.
The comparison challenges the affirmative's inference from sincere multiple witnesses by presenting structurally similar testimony that the affirmative does not accept.
Bass's answer that Christianity has multiple witnesses whereas Islam and Mormonism rest on only one supernatural witness.
After Bass contrasts Christianity's witness count with other religions, Ehrman disputes the Mormon characterization and uses continuing witness claims as a consistency test.
Impartial historical reasoning cannot privilege Christian appearance sources when comparable non-Christian eyewitness claims meet the same proposed criteria.
This states the skeptical methodological objection in full: the affirmative's source-based reasoning appears unable to admit Christian testimony while excluding the Moroni comparison.
Bass's reliance on Paul and inferred testimony from Peter and James as sufficient historical support for resurrection appearances.
The speakers dispute how many direct Christian sources exist, after which Ehrman frames historical impartiality as evaluating sources without using faith commitments to select them.
Later Marian appearance claims differ from the first resurrection experiences because their surrounding religious expectations reduce their evidential surprise.
The move supplies the affirmative's principal distinction between resurrection testimony and a major class of allegedly comparable later visionary reports.
Ehrman's use of reported Marian appearances as a parallel capable of undermining Bass's treatment of resurrection testimony.
When Ehrman raises abundant modern reports of Mary, Bass argues that such claims arise within communities already prepared for saintly appearances and asks about their implications.
Reports of Mary are often unexpected too, so surprise does not distinguish them, and an experience can generate belief without its object appearing.
This attacks the affirmative's proposed discriminator and separates the occurrence of an experience from the conclusion that the perceived supernatural figure objectively appeared.
Bass's contention that Marian visions lack the unexpectedness characteristic of the earliest claimed appearances of Jesus.
The discussion focuses on whether prior worldview makes Marian reports expected and then shifts to what witnesses actually perceived in both Marian and resurrection cases.
Unexpected resurrection belief can arise after initial visionary experiences and subsequent social reinforcement without an actual resurrection.
This concedes a central affirmative premise while denying its inference, offering a natural historical pathway from individual experiences to multiplying communal claims.
Bass's argument that an unexpected crucified-and-risen Messiah claim required an experience best explained by Jesus actually appearing.
The moderator isolates the unexpectedness argument, and Ehrman responds that some followers likely thought they saw Jesus before additional claims spread among the community.
Apocalyptic Jewish beliefs about embodied afterlife explain why followers who thought they saw Jesus alive inferred that God had raised him.
This provides the skeptical side's direct causal explanation for the resurrection conclusion, connecting perceived appearances to an available Jewish conceptual framework.
Bass's claim that the unprecedented resurrection conclusion itself points toward the reality of Jesus's bodily resurrection.
After discussing whether the messianic interpretation followed the experiences, Ehrman reconstructs how disappointed followers could infer bodily resurrection from perceived postmortem encounters.
Jewish alternatives allowed continued heavenly existence until a final resurrection, making the claim that Jesus had already risen especially unexpected.
This directly contests the skeptical causal account by arguing that existing Jewish categories did not naturally yield an individual Messiah's immediate bodily resurrection.
Ehrman's explanation that apocalyptic Jewish embodiment beliefs naturally produced the inference that God had raised Jesus.
At the core boundary, Bass answers Ehrman's worldview explanation by contrasting exalted continued existence and future general resurrection with the early Christian claim about Jesus.
Reports of postmortem appearances do not identify what witnesses actually experienced and admit multiple ordinary explanations.
The move supplies the principal naturalistic alternative to treating the early appearance reports as evidence that Jesus physically rose.
The pro position that early witnesses experienced the physically resurrected Jesus.
After the break, the moderator asks what the disciples and Paul probably experienced if their reports do not establish a bodily resurrection.
Ordinary bereavement-vision explanations do not account for an enemy of the movement experiencing Jesus and converting.
The challenge targets whether the proposed natural mechanism can explain Paul, a pivotal hostile witness rather than a bereaved follower.
Ehrman's claim that familiar postmortem visions provide ordinary parallels for the appearances.
Immediately after Ehrman lists dreams, hallucinations, mistakes, and other possibilities, Bass argues that Paul is unlike typical bereaved experiencers.
Paul already knew the Christian resurrection claim, and guilt or related psychology could have generated a converting vision.
This move directly answers the hostile-witness argument by explaining how Paul could sincerely convert without an objective resurrection appearance.
Bass's contention that Paul's hostility makes an ordinary psychologically generated vision implausible.
Bass presses the special difficulty of Paul seeing someone he opposed; Ehrman answers that Paul knew the claim before meeting leading disciples.
Historical probability favors mistaken perception over a uniquely reported violation of physical law.
The argument states the skeptical methodological basis for rejecting resurrection as the most probable explanation of the appearance testimony.
Bass's request for why Ehrman does not accept Paul's belief that Jesus was raised.
Asked why he thinks Paul was wrong, Ehrman contrasts an unprecedented physical event with familiar testimonial and perceptual error.
The available appearance evidence is at least consistent with resurrection and forms only part of a cumulative case.
This reframes the pro case from testimony alone proving a miracle to appearances supporting resurrection within a broader cumulative argument.
Ehrman's claim that the evidence amounts merely to someone saying that an unprecedented event happened.
Following the demand for extraordinary evidence, Bass says the appearances are not the entire case and argues that they fit what resurrection predicts.
Comparable eyewitness miracle traditions show that reports and resulting conversion do not establish that a miracle occurred.
The analogy tests the consistency of accepting Christian miracle testimony while distrusting similarly structured testimony from another tradition.
Bass's assertion that the appearance evidence supports or is evidentially consistent with Jesus's resurrection.
Ehrman compares the resurrection reports with eyewitness claims about another religious miracle worker and challenges selective acceptance of testimony.
Jesus's singular worldwide worship is an extraordinary historical anomaly that makes his singular resurrection less antecedently dismissible.
The move converts Christianity's extraordinary historical impact into a major component of the cumulative argument for the resurrection explanation.
Ehrman's probability argument that one resurrection among billions is too anomalous for historians to affirm.
After Ehrman contrasts resurrection's rarity with common misperception, Bass argues that the same individual is uniquely worshipped as Lord and God.
The number of people convinced by a miracle claim proves only their conviction, not the truth of the alleged miracle.
This identifies a claimed circularity in using Christianity's success or widespread resurrection belief to establish the resurrection itself.
Bass's argument that Jesus's exceptional influence and worship support the inference that he rose.
As Bass emphasizes Jesus's unparalleled impact, Ehrman separates the historical fact of widespread belief from the truth of its supernatural cause.
Christianity's early growth rate is naturally reproducible and therefore does not indicate a miraculous origin.
The argument directly contests one of the stated bedrock facts by offering a quantitative natural comparison for Christianity's expansion.
Bass's contention that Jesus's extraordinary historical impact is explained well by resurrection.
Ehrman compares Christianity's pre-Constantinian expansion with Mormonism's comparable decadal growth and denies that growth authenticates either faith.
The resurrection claim concerns history's uniquely influential moral and cultural figure, not an otherwise ordinary person.
The move restates the pro side's anomaly argument as a cumulative consideration linking the identity of Jesus with the plausibility of resurrection.
Ehrman's argument that religious growth and influence can be explained without a miraculous beginning.
Asked to explain why Christianity's rise points toward resurrection, Bass stresses the exceptional identity and influence of the person allegedly raised.
Christianity's worldwide expansion fulfills the risen Jesus's stated objective and therefore supports his continuing direction of the church.
This supplies the principal argument connecting the debate's fourth bedrock fact, Christianity's spread, to the claimed historical resurrection.
After the moderator requests an explanation of Christianity's rise, Justin argues that the global fulfillment of Jesus's mission indicates an active risen Lord.
Christianity's later success does not constitute historical evidence about whether Jesus's body returned to life.
The move directly challenges whether a major offered line of support can bear on the debate's central historical resurrection claim.
Justin's claim that Christianity's global success supports the risen Jesus.
Bart separates the movement's subsequent success from the specific historical question of what happened to Jesus's body after crucifixion.
The evidential point is not merely the number of converts but the later fulfillment of the risen Jesus's specific worldwide mission.
This clarification preserves the pro side's expansion argument by distinguishing fulfilled intention from a simple appeal to popularity.
Bart's objection that the number of later believers cannot show what happened to Jesus's body.
Justin reframes his case around a stated objective being realized despite many possible histories in which the Christian movement disappeared.
A religion's growth rate cannot establish either its truth or the historicity of its founder's resurrection.
It rejects the inferential bridge from Christianity's expansion to resurrection, directly contesting one of the pro side's designated bedrock arguments.
Justin's argument that worldwide Christian growth fulfills a prediction and supports the resurrection.
Following Justin's fulfillment clarification, Bart denies that the subsequent growth of a religion supplies historical confirmation of its truth claims.
Recurring visions of Jesus across cultures and centuries, including among non-Christians who convert, provide another line of resurrection evidence.
This introduces and develops a distinct affirmative line explicitly offered as evidence that Jesus rose and continues appearing to people.
Justin describes reports of Jesus visions among Muslims and other groups, treats their breadth as distinctive, and connects them to Jesus's continuing activity.
Dreams do not establish that their objects are real, and comparable vision and healing traditions occur outside Christianity.
The move directly rebuts the new visions argument both epistemically and comparatively, denying its claimed uniqueness and evidential force.
Justin's claim that widespread cross-cultural visions of Jesus uniquely support his continuing risen activity.
Bart argues that dream content need not be real and invokes ancient testimony concerning Asclepius and other cults as comparative counterexamples.
Cross-religious visions disproportionately concern Jesus rather than rival religious figures, making the phenomenon distinctively supportive of Christianity.
This supplies the pro side's direct answer to the objection that religious visions are common and therefore nondiscriminating evidence.
Bart's contention that visions occur in many religions and therefore do not uniquely support Christianity.
Justin distinguishes ordinary within-tradition visions from reports in which adherents of other faiths see Jesus and subsequently move toward Christianity.
Only appearance reports are potentially historical evidence, but testimony from a few witnesses cannot establish an event contrary to consistently observed physical regularities.
This states the con side's governing evidential standard and applies it directly to the resurrection appearances at the heart of the motion.
Justin's cumulative case from crucifixion, messianic claims, appearances, Christian expansion, and later visions.
Bart narrows the relevant material to appearance claims, then argues by analogy that limited testimony is inadequate for an otherwise unprecedented occurrence.
The cumulative pattern of appearances, Christianity's historical expansion, fulfilled intentions, and continuing visions points back to a real resurrection.
This is the pro side's closing synthesis of multiple offered facts into a cumulative inference supporting the debate's resurrection proposition.
Bart's objections that the offered phenomena are theological, nonunique, or insufficient to establish resurrection.
Justin closes by combining the debated appearances, worldwide developments, fulfilled aims, and modern visions into a single cumulative resurrection inference.
Resurrection apologetics improperly substitutes theological reasoning for the critical source evaluation and probability judgments required by historical inquiry.
This closing move states the con side's overarching reason for rejecting the affirmative case as a historical demonstration of resurrection.
Justin's cumulative inference that appearances, expansion, fulfilled aims, and visions historically support resurrection.
Bart concludes by distinguishing past reality from what historians can establish and insists that resurrection claims require critical historical rather than religious argument.
